Today we are splitting ⁦Ghostty's⁩ core into a library. The app you run keeps its window, its fonts and its configuration; the terminal underneath becomes something another program can embed.
A host hands libghostty a native surface and a size, and gets back a grid of cells it can draw however it likes. Input arrives as an event queue, not as callbacks into the ⁦host's⁩ event loop.
What does: everything that used to assume it owned a window.
An event queue instead of callbacks is the whole design in one sentence.
The ABI is versioned by struct size, so an embedder built against an older header keeps working until it asks for a field that did not exist yet.
libghostty splits Ghostty's core out of the app so another frontend can embed the terminal without the macOS shell.
The ABI is deliberately narrow: a surface, a grid of cells and an input queue, with no windowing or font policy in the library.
Commenters split on whether a stable C ABI is worth the loss of Zig's comptime ergonomics inside the core.
The library owns the grid; the host owns the surface. Fonts are the host's, which is why the cell metrics come in through the surface rather than through the config.
That is the right line, but it means the host has to do shaping and fallback, and that is where most of the bugs in a terminal actually live.
Shaping is the part I would happily hand to HarfBuzz and never think about again.
Until you need a fallback chain for emoji and the shaping library disagrees with the system about which font wins.
The versioning story is the part I would want written down before anyone embeds this. Struct size is fine until someone reorders a field.
Versioning by struct size is the one thing here I would copy from Vulkan without hesitation.
